ionic-compounds-valence-s1.title: Ions in three solid samples
ionic-compounds-valence-s1.html: Key: small blue circle, cation (charge shown); larger green or orange circle, anion (charge shown). Each box is a small piece of a much larger solid.

items.q: Which box could represent magnesium chloride?
options: Box 2
Box 3
Box 1
Boxes 1 and 3 both could

why.correct: Magnesium (group 2) forms Mg²⁺; chlorine (group 17) forms Cl⁻. Two Cl⁻ balance one Mg²⁺: MgCl₂, the ratio in Box 1.
options: Box 2 has 1+ cations, but magnesium forms 2+ ions.
Chloride is 1−, not 2−.
Right: Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ in a 1 : 2 ratio, so the charges cancel: MgCl₂.
Box 3 has 2− anions, and chloride is 1−. Box 1 matches: 2+ cations and 1− anions in a 1 : 2 ratio.
MgO: a 2+ cation and a 2− anion, 1 : 1
Mg₂O₂: two of each ion in each formula
NaCl: a 1+ cation and a 1− anion, 1 : 1
MgCl₂: twice as many anions as cations

why.correct: Equal numbers of 2+ and 2− ions: a 1 : 1 ratio, like MgO.
options: Right: +2 and −2 cancel one for one.
A formula gives the simplest ratio; 2 : 2 reduces to 1 : 1.
Box 3's ions carry charges of 2+ and 2−.
Box 3 has equal numbers of cations and anions.

items.q: Why does every box contain cations and anions in the ratio it does?
options: Each cation can touch two anions at a time
Larger ions are outnumbered by smaller ones
The ions are counted by mass, so heavier ions appear less often
The charges cancel, so each solid is neutral

why.correct: An ionic compound is electrically neutral. Box 1: 4(+2) + 8(−1) = 0; Box 2: 6(+1) + 6(−1) = 0; Box 3: 6(+2) + 6(−2) = 0.
options: How ions touch is about packing, not about the formula ratio.
In Boxes 2 and 3 the numbers are equal; the charges decide the ratio.
The ratio counts ions, not masses.
Right: the ratio is set by the charges, so the whole solid has no net charge.

items.q: A student draws calcium nitride (Ca²⁺ and N³⁻) as a box with equal numbers of each ion. What is wrong with the drawing?
options: Nitrogen forms no ions, so it does not belong in the box
Its charges do not cancel; Ca₃N₂ has 3 Ca²⁺ per 2 N³⁻
The ratio should be 2 Ca²⁺ to 3 N³⁻, Ca₂N₃
Calcium ions should carry a 1+ charge

why.correct: Find the smallest numbers that make the charges cancel: 3 × (+2) = +6 and 2 × (−3) = −6. Ca₃N₂.
options: Nitrogen, in group 15, gains 3 electrons to form N³⁻.
That gives 2(+2) + 3(−3) = −5: not neutral.
Calcium is in group 2 and forms Ca²⁺.

items.q: A piece of the Box 1 solid contains 3.0 × 10²² cations. How many anions does it contain?

mistakes.why: Value: there are twice as many anions as cations, not half as many.

why.correct: The ratio of cations to anions is 1 : 2, so 2 × 3.0 × 10²² = 6.0 × 10²² anions.

items.q: What ion does sulfur most commonly form?
options: S⁶⁺
S²⁺
S⁻
S²⁻

why.correct: Sulfur has 6 valence electrons. Gaining 2 reaches the noble gas configuration of argon: S²⁻.
options: Losing 6 valence electrons would take far more energy than gaining 2.
Nonmetals at the right of the table gain electrons rather than lose them.
One electron leaves sulfur one short of argon's configuration.
Right: gaining 2 electrons gives [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶, the configuration of argon.

items.q: Why does aluminum form Al³⁺ and not Al⁴⁺?
options: A 4th electron would come from the core, costing far more energy
Aluminum has three electrons in total
A 4+ charge is too large for any ion to carry
Aluminum wants to have exactly three electrons fewer than before

why.correct: Al: [Ne] 3s² 3p¹. Losing the 3 valence electrons is affordable; a 4th would come from the 2p core, close to the nucleus and poorly shielded.
options: Right: after 3 electrons, Al³⁺ has neon's configuration; the next is a tightly held core electron.
Aluminum has 13 electrons; 3 of them are valence electrons.
The limit comes from the energy to remove core electrons, not from a fixed maximum charge.
Atoms do not want things; the energy cost of removing each electron sets the charge.

items.q: Which pair of ions from these elements has the same electron configuration as argon?
options: Li⁺ and Br⁻
Al³⁺ and S²⁻
Ca²⁺ and S²⁻
Ca²⁺ and Br⁻

why.correct: Argon has 18 electrons. Ca²⁺ (20 − 2) and S²⁻ (16 + 2) both have 18: they are isoelectronic with argon.
options: Li⁺ matches helium (2 electrons) and Br⁻ matches krypton (36).
Al³⁺ has 10 electrons, like neon.
Right: Ca loses 2 (20 → 18 electrons) and S gains 2 (16 → 18).
Br⁻ has 36 electrons, like krypton.

items.q: What is the formula of the compound formed by aluminum and bromine?
options: Al₃Br
AlBr
AlBr₃
Al₂Br₃
This puts the 3 on the wrong ion: 3(+3) + (−1) = +8.
One Br⁻ would leave the compound with a 2+ charge.
Right: Al³⁺ and Br⁻; three Br⁻ balance one Al³⁺.
That would need Al with a charge of 3/2, which does not exist.

items.q: Sodium and potassium both react with water in similar ways. Which explanation is best?
options: Both have one loosely held s valence electron
They have similar masses
They have the same number of protons
They have the same number of shells

why.correct: Elements in a group share the same valence configuration (here ns¹), so they gain or lose electrons in the same way and react alike.
options: Right: same group, same number of valence electrons, so similar chemistry.
Potassium is much heavier than sodium; mass is not the reason.
Na has 11 and K has 19.
K has four occupied shells and Na three.

items.q: Which formulas are correct for compounds of the ions shown? Select all that apply.
options: K₂O (K⁺, O²⁻)
CaF (Ca²⁺, F⁻)
Na₂N (Na⁺, N³⁻)
MgO₂ (Mg²⁺, O²⁻)

why.correct: Choose the smallest whole numbers of each ion that make the total charge zero.
options: This leaves a 1+ charge; the formula is CaF₂.
This gives 2(+1) − 3 = −1; the formula is Na₃N.
This gives +2 − 4 = −2; the formula is MgO.

items.q: A sodium atom becomes a Na⁺ ion. Predict how each quantity changes.

variables.name: Number of protons
variables.why: Losing an electron does not change the nucleus.

variables.name: Radius
variables.why: Na⁺ has lost its only shell-3 electron, so its outermost electrons are in shell 2.

variables.name: Number of electrons in the outermost occupied shell
variables.why: The outermost occupied shell is now shell 2, with 8 electrons, instead of shell 3 with 1.

why.correct: Na (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹) → Na⁺ (1s² 2s² 2p⁶): same protons, a smaller particle, and a filled outer shell of 8.

items.q: Put the steps for writing the formula of an ionic compound in order.
options: Find each element's group to get its valence electrons
Write the charge each ion forms
Choose the smallest numbers of ions whose charges add to zero
Write the cation first, then the anion, with those numbers as subscripts

why.correct: Valence electrons → ion charges → balance the charges → write cation then anion, e.g. Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ → CaCl₂.

items.q: A student writes the formula of the compound of magnesium and nitrogen as MgN. Which reasoning shows the error?
options: Magnesium and nitrogen form a molecule, not ions
The formula should list nitrogen first, since it is the anion
Mg forms Mg³⁺ to match N³⁻, so MgN is right
Mg²⁺ and N³⁻ give a net −1; Mg₃N₂ is neutral

why.correct: Write the charges, then balance them: Mg²⁺ × 3 = +6 and N³⁻ × 2 = −6, Mg₃N₂.
options: A metal from group 2 and a nonmetal from group 15 form ions.
The cation is written first.
Magnesium, in group 2, forms Mg²⁺.

items.q: Which ion is isoelectronic with (has the same number of electrons as) neon?
options: Mg²⁺
Ca²⁺
Cl⁻
K⁺

why.correct: Neon has 10 electrons. Mg (12) minus 2 gives 10.
options: Right: 12 − 2 = 10 electrons, like neon.
Ca²⁺ has 18 electrons, like argon.
Cl⁻ has 18 electrons, like argon.
K⁺ has 18 electrons, like argon.
